state.misconception_label: Assumes that an arrow on a number line starts at zero

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: ![Number line with -12 and -7 marked. Starting at -12, follow an arrow pointing to the right labelled +10. Then there is an arrow labelled b pointing to the left, which ends at -7 on the number line.]() What is the value of \( b \) ? I got \( -7 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you walk me through your thought process when determining the value of \( b \)? What assumptions did you make about the direction of the arrows on the number line and their starting points?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Well, I thought the arrow always starts at zero, so when I saw the arrow pointing to the right for +10, I just added that to -12. But then for the arrow labelled \( b \), I thought it just went to -7 from there. So I’m a bit confused about where the arrows actually start. Can you help me understand that better?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think of any examples where the starting point of an arrow on a number line is not at zero? How might considering different starting points for the arrows change your approach to finding the value of \( b \)?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I guess I can see that the arrows can start at different points, not just zero. Like, if I think about the first arrow starting at -12, then when it goes +10, it actually ends at -2, right? But I'm still confused about how to figure out where the second arrow starts from. Does it always start from the end of the first arrow?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the specific misconception about arrows starting at zero through targeted questioning, and the student shows clear progress from assuming arrows start at zero to correctly calculating the first arrow's endpoint at -2, though they still need guidance on the second arrow.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student's thinking about arrow starting points and never directly provides the answer, which is a textbook example of the Socratic method.
